correctness.rationale: For every fixed mean μ>0 and t∈[0,μ], all distributions are normalized and have finite exponential moments. Differentiating the compound-Poisson Lévy coefficients produces nonnegative convex-test brackets and strict ordering for strictly convex tests. A positive all-index partial-sum identity proves mass log-concavity, and the entropy score derivative is strictly positive in the interior. Exact generating-function derivatives yield both endpoint expansions. The geometric reference score has mean zero and squared norm 1/(1+μ); the Poisson coefficient is E log[(N+2)/(N+1)]/2. Uniform geometric-tail bounds justify finite/infinite sum interchange and the local expansion; a standalone numerical checker passed and is explicitly not the infinite proof.

originality.rationale: The object is the long-known shape-one Delaporte convolution, and the general entropy-from-convex-order theorem is prior art. The asserted incremental result is the simultaneous strict entropy interpolation for its fixed-mean slice with two exact endpoint quadratic coefficients, in particular the nontrivial Poisson expectation and the rational geometric coefficient. Searches under PoiG, Poisson–geometric convolution, Delaporte and relative-entropy/endpoint-curvature aliases found no same-claim implication in accessible publications or published published-finding corpus summaries. This is a best-knowledge, same-model priority assessment, not an assertion of exhaustive historical uniqueness. value.rationale: At fixed expected count, dispersion variance μ+t² grows while entropy moves strictly between canonical Poisson and geometric count models. The exact quadratic coefficients describe quantitatively how slowly information changes near each extreme, rather than merely asserting an unquantified entropy inequality. The exact two-sided sensitivity is a natural, standalone characteristic for comparing overdispersed count models; it is not a routine special case of the abstract Yu entropy theorem, which provides no such coefficients.
